questions.text: A large new technology campus has been constructed and is now operating in the Hamilton region. On Graph One, explain each shift (aggregate supply and aggregate demand curves) shown, and the impact on economic growth.
questions.expectedAnswer: AD shifts right (increased investment spending during construction, consumption from workers and visitors). AS shifts right (increased productive capacity from the new campus). Both shifts increase Real GDP, contributing to economic growth.
questions.markingGuide: Explains both shifts — AD right (investment/consumption) and AS right (productive capacity) — and links to economic growth (increased Real GDP).

questions.text: Explain one disadvantage of using real GDP to measure economic growth.
questions.expectedAnswer: Real GDP does not account for environmental degradation — GDP could increase while pollution and resource depletion worsen, meaning true wellbeing may not have improved.
questions.markingGuide: Identifies a valid limitation of using real GDP as a measure of growth.

questions.text: Compare and contrast the impact of the new technology campus on different regional growth rates in New Zealand.
questions.expectedAnswer: The Waikato region benefits directly through increased employment, technology sector spending, and business activity related to the campus. Other regions may benefit indirectly from supply chain linkages and knowledge transfer. However, the concentrated investment in Hamilton could widen regional inequality, as other regions do not receive the same level of development.
questions.markingGuide: Compares Waikato growth with other regions, assessing both direct and indirect impacts.

questions.text: Compare and contrast the impact of the new technology campus on the distribution of income in the Hamilton area.
questions.expectedAnswer: High-income earners (tech professionals, property owners near the campus) benefit most through high salaries and capital gains. Low-income earners gain employment in service roles such as cleaning, catering, and transport, but these tend to be lower-paid jobs. Income inequality may widen despite overall growth.
questions.markingGuide: Compares and contrasts impact on different income groups in the Hamilton area.

questions.text:
Referring to the circular flow model, identify three flows that will increase due to growth in New Zealand's technology exports.

Flow 1:
Flow 2:
Flow 3:
questions.expectedAnswer: Any three from: Export receipts (from overseas sector to firms), Consumption spending (from households to firms), Tax revenue (from households/firms to government), Investment (from financial sector to firms).
questions.markingGuide: Three valid flows identified from the circular flow model.

questions.text: Choose one of the flows identified in (a) and explain why it will increase due to growth in technology exports.
questions.expectedAnswer: Export receipts increase because overseas buyers pay for New Zealand technology products and services. This represents an injection into the circular flow, increasing total income in the economy.
questions.markingGuide: Explains why the chosen flow increases with reference to technology exports and the circular flow model.

questions.text: Referring to the circular flow model, explain why a large overseas technology firm setting up operations in New Zealand might increase growth more than a domestic firm expanding.
questions.expectedAnswer: An overseas firm brings new investment capital from outside the circular flow as an injection (foreign investment). A domestic firm expanding only redistributes existing income within the circular flow — their investment comes from domestic savings. New money from overseas increases total income in the economy.
questions.markingGuide: Explains that overseas investment creates an injection while domestic expansion redistributes existing income.

questions.text: Compare and contrast the impact of increased technology exports on government revenue and expenditure.
questions.expectedAnswer: Government revenue increases through income tax from tech sector employees, company tax from profitable tech firms, and GST on increased spending. Government expenditure may also increase due to need for digital infrastructure, education funding, and research grants. The net effect depends on whether additional revenue exceeds additional costs.
questions.markingGuide: Compares revenue (taxes) with expenditure (infrastructure/services) and assesses the net effect.

questions.text: Compare and contrast the impact of increased technology exports on local residents and businesses in the accommodation sector in a city hosting a major tech hub.
questions.expectedAnswer: Accommodation businesses benefit from increased demand from visiting clients and relocating workers, expanding operations and raising profits. Residents may benefit from more job opportunities and improved services. However, residents may face higher rental costs, increased traffic, and pressure on local housing. A shortage of affordable housing and gentrification are potential negative impacts.
questions.markingGuide: Compares and contrasts impacts on residents (mixed) vs businesses (mostly positive), with specific examples.

questions.text:
In early 2023, a severe drought caused extensive damage to farmland, irrigation systems, and rural infrastructure across several regions. When productive assets are damaged, New Zealand's productive capacity decreases.

Explain why a natural disaster such as severe drought leads to lower GDP. Include a definition of GDP in your answer.
questions.expectedAnswer: GDP is the total value of goods and services produced in a country over a given period. Drought destroys productive farmland and irrigation infrastructure, reducing the economy's ability to produce agricultural goods and services, which lowers GDP.
questions.markingGuide: Defines GDP and explains how drought damage reduces productive capacity and output.

questions.text: On Graph Two, a production possibility frontier (PPF) shows consumer goods on one axis and agricultural goods on the other. Label the opportunity cost of increasing government spending to fund drought recovery.
questions.expectedAnswer: Label the decrease in consumer goods when resources are redirected to agricultural recovery — the opportunity cost is the forgone consumer goods.
questions.markingGuide: Opportunity cost correctly labelled as the reduction in consumer goods when moving along the PPF.

questions.text: Referring to Graph Two, explain why there is an opportunity cost of increasing government spending to fund drought recovery.
questions.expectedAnswer: Resources are scarce. When the government increases spending to fund drought recovery, resources are diverted from producing consumer goods. The economy must trade off consumer goods production for agricultural recovery because resources cannot be used for both simultaneously.
questions.markingGuide: Explains scarcity and trade-off — more agricultural recovery means fewer consumer goods, with reference to the PPF.

questions.text: Graph Three shows a future PPF (labelled X*) if the government does invest heavily in drought recovery (point B). Draw a future PPF (Y*) that would result if the government does not invest in recovery (point A).
questions.expectedAnswer: Draw Y* as a PPF that is closer to the origin than X* but still outside the current PPF, showing less growth without drought recovery investment.
questions.markingGuide: Y* drawn between the current PPF and X*, showing less growth than operating at point B.

questions.text: Referring to Graph Three, explain why the future PPF (Y*) you have drawn shows a different level of potential capacity from the future PPF (X*) created by investing in drought recovery.
questions.expectedAnswer: At point B, more resources go to drought recovery and rebuilding irrigation systems, increasing future productive capacity more than at point A. Restored farmland and improved water management enable more efficient production, shifting the future PPF outward more. At point A, without recovery, damaged farmland limits future agricultural productivity, so Y* is closer to the origin than X*.
questions.markingGuide: Explains why different investment levels lead to different future PPF positions — more recovery investment creates greater future capacity.
